title: Nuclear Radioactivity
lead: Some nuclei are radioactive: they decay of their own accord and emit rays from the nucleus. This section tells how radioactivity was discovered, how a magnetic field sorts its rays into alpha, beta and gamma, and why all three ionize the matter they cross yet travel such different distances through it.
objectives: Explain the types of radiation—alpha emission, beta emission, and gamma emission.
Explain the ionization of radiation in an atom.
summary_html:
• Some nuclei are radioactive—they spontaneously decay destroying some part of their mass and emitting energetic rays, a process called nuclear radioactivity.
  • Nuclear radiation, like x rays, is ionizing radiation, because energy sufficient to ionize matter is emitted in each decay.
  • The range (or distance traveled in a material) of ionizing radiation is directly related to the charge of the emitted particle and its energy, with greater-charge and lower-energy particles having the shortest ranges.
  • Radiation detectors are based directly or indirectly upon the ionization created by radiation, as are the effects of radiation on living and inert materials.
notes: The PhET link Beta Decay, whose description is of building an atom from protons, neutrons and electrons, is left out.

figures.original_caption: Alpha, beta, and gamma rays are passed through a magnetic field on the way to a phosphorescent screen. The αs and βs bend in opposite directions, while the γs are unaffected, indicating a positive charge for αs, negative for βs, and neutral for γs. Consistent results are obtained with electric fields. Collection of the radiation offers further confirmation from the direct measurement of excess charge.

The penetration or range of radiation depends on its energy, the material it encounters, and the type of radiation. (a) Greater energy means greater range. (b) Radiation has a smaller range in materials with high electron density. (c) Alphas have the smallest range, betas have a greater range, and gammas penetrate the farthest.

exercises.prompt: A nucleus is observed to emit a $\gamma$ ray with a frequency of $6.3\times 10^{19}\;\text{Hz}$. What must happen to the nucleus as a consequence?

options: The nucleus must also emit an α particle of energy 0.26 MeV in the opposite direction.
The nucleus must also emit a β particle of energy 0.26 MeV in the opposite direction.
answer.hint: Find the photon’s energy from $\kE = hf$ with $h = 4.14\times 10^{-15}\;\text{eV}\cdot\text{s}$, and ask where that energy comes from.

exercises.prompt: Suppose the range for a 5.0-MeV $\alpha$ ray is known to be 2.0 mm in a certain material. Does this mean that every 5.0-MeV $\alpha$ ray that strikes this material travels 2.0 mm, or does the range have an average value with some statistical fluctuations in the distances traveled? Explain.

answer.solution: The range is an average. An $\alpha$ loses its energy in a great many separate ionizing collisions, and both the energy taken in each collision and the number of collisions along a given length vary by chance. Two $\alpha$s of the same energy therefore stop at slightly different depths, scattered about 2.0 mm. Because each $\alpha$ makes so many ionizations, the chance variations largely average out, so the spread is small compared with the range itself, and the range is still a useful, well-defined number, unlike the range of $\gamma$ rays.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between $\gamma$ rays and characteristic x rays? Is either necessarily more energetic than the other? Which can be the most energetic?

answer.solution: They differ only in their source: a $\gamma$ ray comes from the de-excitation of a nucleus, and a characteristic x ray from the de-excitation of an atom when an inner-shell vacancy is filled. At the same energy the two photons are identical, so neither is necessarily more energetic; a low-energy $\gamma$ ray of a few tens of keV carries less energy than the characteristic x rays of a heavy element. Nuclear energies, however, reach the order of $10^{6}\;\text{eV}$, more than ten times the most energetic characteristic x rays, so the most energetic of the two are $\gamma$ rays.

exercises.prompt: Ionizing radiation interacts with matter by scattering from electrons and nuclei in the substance. Based on the law of conservation of momentum and energy, explain why electrons tend to absorb more energy than nuclei in these interactions.

answer.solution: In a collision the radiation gives the struck particle some momentum $\kdp$, and a particle of mass $m$ that starts at rest then has kinetic energy $(\kdp)^{2}/2m$. For a given push, the energy taken is larger the smaller the mass. An electron’s mass is thousands of times smaller than a nucleus’s, so it carries away far more energy from the same kind of encounter; a heavy nucleus recoils slowly and takes little, much as a ball bouncing off a wall keeps nearly all its energy. Momentum and energy conservation therefore send most of the radiation’s energy into the electrons.

exercises.prompt: What characteristics of radioactivity show it to be nuclear in origin and not atomic?

answer.solution: First, radioactivity belongs to certain elements and does not change with the chemical state of the element, nor with its temperature, pressure or state of ionization. All of these affect the electrons of an atom, so the radiation cannot come from electron transitions. Second, each event releases an energy of the order of $10^{6}\;\text{eV}$, far more than the few eV of atomic and chemical processes and more than ten times the most energetic characteristic x rays.

exercises.prompt: What is the source of the energy emitted in radioactive decay? Identify an earlier conservation law, and describe how it was modified to take such processes into account.

answer.solution: The energy comes from the conversion of a small part of the nucleus’s mass into energy, as $\kE = m\kc^{2}$ relates them. A radioactive source emits energy continuously with no energy put in, which seemed to violate the law of conservation of energy. The law was kept by counting mass as a form of energy: what is conserved is the total of the energy and the rest energy $m\kc^{2}$, so the mass the nucleus loses reappears as the energy of its radiation.

exercises.prompt: Consider Figure 31.3. If an electric field is substituted for the magnetic field with positive charge instead of the north pole and negative charge instead of the south pole, in which directions will the $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ rays bend?

answer.solution: An electric field points from the positive plate to the negative one, and pushes a positive charge along the field and a negative charge against it, unlike a magnetic field, which pushes sideways. So the $\alpha$s, being positive, bend toward the negative plate, where the south pole was; the $\beta$s, being negative, bend toward the positive plate, where the north pole was; and the uncharged $\gamma$s go straight. The $\alpha$s and $\beta$s still bend in opposite directions, but now along the line joining the plates rather than across it.

exercises.prompt: Explain how an $\alpha$ particle can have a larger range in air than a $\beta$ particle with the same energy in lead.

answer.solution: Range depends on the material as well as on the type of radiation. At the same energy an $\alpha$ ionizes more readily than a $\beta$, since it has twice the charge and moves much more slowly, so in the same material it stops first. But radiation loses its energy mainly to electrons, and lead has thousands of times more electrons in each cubic centimeter than air. A $\beta$ in lead meets so many electrons that it stops in about a millimeter, while an $\alpha$ in thin air meets so few that it travels a few centimeters.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the following according to their ability to act as radiation shields, with the best first and worst last. Explain your ordering in terms of how radiation loses its energy in matter. (a) A solid material with low density composed of low-mass atoms. (b) A gas composed of high-mass atoms. (c) A gas composed of low-mass atoms. (d) A solid with high density composed of high-mass atoms.

answer.solution: Radiation loses its energy by ionizing, mostly by giving energy to electrons, so the best shield packs the most electrons into each unit of volume. A solid is roughly a thousand times denser than a gas, so both solids come before both gases; within each pair, high-mass atoms carry more electrons each, and a dense solid of them packs the most. The order is (d), (a), (b), (c): the dense solid of high-mass atoms best, then the light solid, then the gas of heavy atoms, and the gas of light atoms worst.

exercises.prompt: Often, when people have to work around radioactive materials spills, we see them wearing white coveralls (usually a plastic material). What types of radiation (if any) do you think these suits protect the worker from, and how?

answer.solution: A thin plastic suit stops $\alpha$ radiation, whose range is like that of a sheet of paper, and it absorbs some low-energy $\beta$s, but $\gamma$ rays pass straight through it. Its main protection is against contamination: it keeps radioactive dust and liquid off the skin and clothes, so the worker does not carry the material away or take it into the body, where even short-range $\alpha$ and $\beta$ emitters do harm. The suit is taken off and disposed of with the contamination on it.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts. A 2.00-T magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the path of charged particles in a bubble chamber. What is the radius of curvature of the path of a 10 MeV proton in this field? Neglect any slowing along its path.

answer.hint: Find the proton’s speed from its kinetic energy, $\frac{1}{2}m\kv^{2} = 10\;\text{MeV}$, which is classical at this speed, then use $\kr = m\kv/(\kq\kBmag)$.
